1. # **INTRODUCTION**

   1. ## **Project Context**

Around the world, the movement of people and goods is being reshaped by an ongoing shift toward digital operations, with vehicle fleets, trip scheduling, and fare payment increasingly migrating onto intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and analytics-driven fleet management \[1\], \[2\], \[3\]. To enhance operational efficiency and prevent vehicle overloading, modern public transportation systems are increasingly integrating automated monitoring technologies, such as real-time passenger counting systems that use Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and YOLOv8 models to optimize capacity and improve passenger comfort \[4\]. Furthermore, international transit operators use intelligent tracking algorithms to automatically monitor passengers entering and exiting, thereby enhancing fare-evasion control and reducing financial losses \[5\]. In the Philippine context, the same shift is being propelled by government policy through the Department of Transportation's Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP), which identifies route-network efficiency and fleet management as principal reform objectives \[6\]. While the widespread adoption of app-based services such as Transport Network Vehicle Services (TNVS) has recalibrated passenger expectations toward digitally coordinated, on-demand travel \[7\], \[8\], van operations based at terminals running fixed routes franchised by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) continue to rely heavily on paper records. This leaves them severely detached from the automated capacity management and digital auditing tools that have become standard across the rest of the transport sector \[9\].  
Based on an operational assessment and an interview with the manager of the A2Z Transport Cooperative Van Terminal, the association currently relies on a highly manual dispatching system. Vans depart along fixed LTFRB-approved routes, with terminal dispatchers physically queuing passengers, assigning seats, and recording departure headcounts into handwritten logbooks. As an integral part of the association's workflow, the inter-city van remittance process follows strict cooperative rules to ensure passenger manifesting, cash safety, and alignment with terminal rotation. Under this manual system, drivers and conductors are required to surrender all collected cash fares to the terminal office at the end of their route rotation and manually cross-reference the surrendered cash against the physical dispatch logs to clear their accounts. Meanwhile, official trip schedules are communicated primarily via static physical tarpaulins posted at the terminal. To reserve seats, passengers are forced to navigate highly fragmented communication channels, relying on a disorganized mix of Facebook Messenger, SMS, and direct phone calls to coordinate with dispatchers.

This reliance on manual recording and fragmented communication creates three persistent gaps that negatively impact both the cooperative and the traveling public. First, the manual dispatching process makes the association vulnerable to revenue leakage. Because the remittance process relies entirely on the integrity of paper records, walk-in passengers are frequently boarded without being entered into the logbook. Consequently, these fares are easily hidden during the end-of-shift remittance, resulting in undocumented transactions that bypass formal audit trails. Establishing a centralized digital manifest provides a critical operational benefit to combat this: it creates an immutable baseline of expected vehicle occupancy that can be directly validated against advanced physical monitoring tools, such as intelligent camera-based passenger counting systems \[4\], \[5\]. If a conductor or driver deliberately omits a passenger to pocket the cash fare, comparing the system's live digital manifest with the automated counting data during that specific trip immediately exposes the discrepancy, effectively closing the revenue loop. Second, vans routinely carry passengers beyond the strict 14-seat capacity limit. This practice not only creates direct regulatory risks and LTFRB violations for operators but also severely compromises passenger safety and physical comfort during transit. Third, terminal dispatchers lack a reliable, centralized mechanism to manage passenger no-shows, resulting in disorganized boarding queues and inefficient seat allocation at departure.  
Beyond the operational inefficiencies affecting the cooperative, the manual system creates significant problems for passengers. Because seat reservations are handled informally through disjointed social media threads and direct phone calls, passengers face constant uncertainty regarding seat availability. There is no centralized platform to guarantee a booking, frequently forcing passengers to arrive at the terminal hours early to secure a seat physically. Furthermore, the complete absence of real-time tracking or automated notifications leaves passengers entirely uninformed about vehicle dispatch times, sudden delays, or trip cancellations. This lack of transparency and communication severely degrades the daily transit experience, resulting in wasted time and increased anxiety for the traveling public.

Table 1 presents an analysis of existing transportation management methods, specifically comparing manual dispatching, social media bookings, and active commercial Transport Network Vehicle Service (TNVS) platforms such as Grab and JoyRide

| System | Digital Ticketing | Revenue Audit Trail | Capacity Enforcement (14-seat) | Real-Time Vehicle Tracking | Integrated Passenger-Crew Communication |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Manual Dispatching (Logbook/Tarpaulin) | No | No | Manual/weak | No | No (informal relay only) |
| Social Media Booking (Facebook Messenger) | No | Partial (chat logs) | No | No | Partial (one-way, unstructured messaging) |
| Active TNVS Platforms (e.g., Grab, JoyRide) | Yes (In-app) | Yes | N/A (private hire) | Yes (Per-trip, private hire only) | Partial (in-app chat/call, single trip only) |
| Proposed SabayGo System | Yes | Yes | Yes (Strict 14-seat enforcement) | Yes (Fleet-wide, terminal-level, node-based ETA) | Yes (Structured two-way messaging across all roles) |

It is worth noting that TNVS platforms do provide live GPS tracking and in-app communication; however, both are scoped to a single private hire between one passenger and one driver. This visibility is not exposed to a terminal dispatcher managing a shared fleet across a fixed route, nor does it extend to coordination among a van's own crew. SabayGo's NAHGM module extends tracking to a fleet-wide, node-based view accessible simultaneously to the Operator and every passenger booked on a shared route, while its messaging module provides persistent, structured channels across all four terminal-based roles, replacing the ad hoc mix of Messenger, SMS, and phone calls entirely rather than merely digitizing a single trip's chat. 

As outlined in the matrix, existing applications and methods do not fully meet the operational requirements of terminal-based public utility vans. While active TNVS platforms like Grab and JoyRide excel in digital ticketing and real-time notifications, they utilize dynamic, door-to-door routing, which violates the strict fixed-route compliance mandated by the LTFRB for UV Express units. Furthermore, commercial TNVS applications are designed for private, single-booking hires and lack mechanisms to enforce a shared 14-seat capacity limit or to capture mid-route walk-in boardings at designated terminal nodes. Conversely, while manual dispatching and social media bookings adhere to fixed routes, they completely lack automated revenue audit trails, tamper-evident digital ticketing, and location-based check-in validation. Crucially, none of the existing digital platforms provide offline synchronization capabilities, which is an essential requirement for conductors managing live passenger manifests in connectivity dead zones. These unresolved gaps underscore the need for a specialized system explicitly tailored to the constraints and regulatory framework of cooperative fleet operations.

To resolve the identified operational gaps and passenger pain points, this study develops SabayGo, a comprehensive web and mobile-based booking aggregator and fleet management system engineered specifically for terminal-based public utility vans. Unlike commercial TNVS platforms, the system is designed to adhere strictly to LTFRB fixed-route regulations while digitizing the entire terminal workflow. It introduces QR code digital ticketing to formalize seat reservations \[10\], automated capacity enforcement using pessimistic database locking to strictly prevent overloading beyond 14 passengers, and a simple location-based check-in step to confirm a passenger's physical presence at their designated boarding terminal before boarding. To close the gap between the digital manifest and actual vehicle occupancy — the exact point at which revenue leakage occurs — an in-van AI inference layer running the YOLOv8 object detection model automatically counts the physical passengers on board and cross-validates that count against the digital manifest, extending the camera-based passenger-counting approaches already established in transit contexts \[4\], \[5\]. To close the visibility gap left by static tarpaulin schedules and informal dispatcher relay, a NAHGM (Node-Aligned Haversine Geofenced Monitoring) module continuously tracks each van's live position against its assigned route nodes, providing operators and passengers with real-time location visibility and node-by-node arrival estimates. To close the communication gap created by the terminal's reliance on Facebook Messenger, SMS, and phone calls, the system further introduces a two-way in-app messaging module connecting passengers, conductors, drivers, and the cooperative administrator directly within the platform. Furthermore, it equips conductors with an offline-capable digital manifest to ensure continuous operation in connectivity dead zones. Subsequently, it synchronizes data to maintain a secure, tamper-evident revenue audit trail. 

To directly address the revenue-leakage and transparency gaps identified during the operational assessment, this study centers its technical contribution on two independent intelligence layers rather than on a specialized booking or matching algorithm: an AI-based passenger reconciliation mechanism and a GPS-based live tracking mechanism. Manual dispatch logs can be manipulated because they depend entirely on the honesty of the person recording them; a conductor or driver who boards an undocumented walk-in simply omits that passenger from the log, and no downstream process can detect the missing entry. YOLOv8, a real-time object detection model, resolves this by independently counting the physical occupants of the van from live camera footage, producing a visual passenger count (C\_visual) that exists entirely outside the digital or paper manifest. Comparing this visual count against the manifested booked count (C\_booked) yields a variance (Δ) that immediately exposes any undocumented boarding, regardless of what was or was not entered into the system. Separately, because official trip status is currently communicated only through static tarpaulins and informal dispatcher relay, the terminal has no mechanism to confirm a van's live position or estimated arrival once it departs. NAHGM (Node-Aligned Haversine Geofenced Monitoring) resolves this by continuously computing the Haversine distance between the van's live GPS coordinate and each upcoming route node, producing a live position feed and node-by-node ETA that exists independently of manual relay. Because both mechanisms operate independently of the booking workflow itself, the booking and seat-reservation process can remain a straightforward reservation system — passengers select a route, choose a boarding and alighting terminal, and reserve one of the fourteen available seats — while YOLOv8 supplies the revenue-assurance function and NAHGM supplies the visibility function that the manual process lacks. 

2. ## **Purpose and Description**

The main purpose of this study is to develop a web- and mobile-based public utility van-booking aggregator and fleet management system that digitizes terminal-to-terminal van reservations, ticketing, revenue tracking, live vehicle tracking, and terminal communication for cooperative operations. The system is designed to advance SDG 9 by delivering innovation-driven transport infrastructure and to fulfill the University of Mindanao's institutional thrust on ICT-enabled services for the local industry. 

SabayGo defines four distinct user roles with separate access rights. The passenger uses the mobile application to browse fixed routes and schedules, select a boarding and alighting terminal along the route, book and pay for the corresponding segment, receive a digital QR ticket, complete a location-based check-in at their boarding terminal, view live NAHGM vehicle tracking and node-by-node ETA for their booked trip, exchange two-way messages with the assigned Conductor and the cooperative administrator, and receive real-time delay and cancellation notifications. The Conductor uses a terminal-facing interface to scan passenger QR codes for boarding validation at each stop along the route, log walk-in passengers into the digital manifest, operate an offline-capable manifest that caches data locally in connectivity dead zones and synchronizes upon reconnection, transmit live GPS pings for NAHGM tracking throughout the trip, and exchange two-way messages with passengers, the Driver, and the cooperative administrator. The Operator uses a management dashboard to configure fleet units and schedules; monitor live manifests; trigger and review YOLOv8-based occupancy reconciliation audits; review the revenue audit trail to identify unrecorded boardings; reconcile fare collection; enforce the 14-seat capacity constraint across the fleet; monitor the live NAHGM vehicle-tracking map across the fleet; and exchange two-way messages with conductors, drivers, and passengers. The Driver uses a minimal in-vehicle interface to confirm the onboard passenger count before departing each staffed terminal, issue pre-registered physical QR tickets to cash-paying walk-in passengers at unstaffed stops, transmit live GPS pings for NAHGM tracking throughout the trip, and exchange two-way messages with the Conductor and the cooperative administrator, with all counts and issuances automatically reconciled against the live manifest. 

3. ## **Objectives**

### *1.3.1	General Objective*

The general objective of this study is to design and develop SabayGo, a web and mobile-based booking aggregator and fleet management system for terminal-based public utility vans, using Flutter for the frontend, FastAPI (Python) for the backend, MySQL 8.0 for the database, a YOLOv8-based AI inference layer for automated passenger-count reconciliation, and a NAHGM (Node-Aligned Haversine Geofenced Monitoring) module for continuous live van tracking and node-based ETA estimation. 

*1.3.2	Specific Objectives*  
To achieve the general objective, this study specifically aims to:

1.3.2.1 Provide a location-based check-in process, backed by a database locking mechanism, that prevents double-booking, confirms a passenger's presence at the boarding terminal, and removes unfair no-show penalties.

1.3.2.2 Integrate a live GPS tracking feature, NAHGM, that shows passengers and operators where each van currently is along its route and estimates when it will arrive at each stop.

1.3.2.3 Integrate a passenger headcount detection feature using YOLOv8 that counts the passengers physically on board from cabin camera footage and flags any difference from the digital booking manifest.

1.3.2.4 Create a revenue dashboard that compares booked seats against collected fares, highlights mismatches, and alerts operators to possible revenue loss.

1.3.2.5 Deliver real-time notifications to passengers, conductors, drivers, and the operator for trip delays, cancellations, and boarding confirmations.

4. ## **Scope and Limitation**

This study covers terminal-based, fixed-route public utility van operations on LTFRB-approved routes, with the four defined user roles (Operator, Conductor, Driver, Passenger). The system manages route and schedule configuration; segment-based seat inventory bound to the 14-seat capacity for each route segment; QR-code ticketing; pairwise terminal fare matrices covering any boarding–alighting combination along a route; location-based check-in; NAHGM-based live vehicle tracking and node-by-node ETA; YOLOv8-based passenger-count reconciliation; revenue auditing; real-time push notifications; and two-way in-app messaging among passengers, conductors, drivers, and the cooperative administrator. Intermediate stops may be unstaffed; at such stops, boarding is captured via the cooperative's payment-gateway QR code, driver-issued pre-registered physical tickets, and passenger self-check-in, with post-trip reconciliation controls in place of on-site Conductor validation. Deployment is scoped as a pilot at the A2Z Transport Cooperative's van terminal in the Davao region, with terminal nodes defined by fixed GPS coordinates. 

The system does not perform dynamic or commercial door-to-door routing; routes are fixed, ordered sequences of registered terminal stops, and the system does not support dynamic rerouting, skipped stops, or pickups outside registered terminal nodes. Passenger features that require live data (booking, notifications, check-in) depend on internet and GPS availability on the passenger's device; offline caching is provided only for the Conductor role. Cashless top-ups rely on third-party payment gateways, and the study does not implement its own payment-processing or banking infrastructure. Location validation depends on the accuracy of consumer-grade smartphone GPS and does not include hardware-level anti-spoofing countermeasures beyond distance-threshold logic \[13\]. Similarly, the NAHGM tracking module depends on a continuous data connection and periodic GPS pings from the driver or conductor's device; tracking accuracy and update frequency are bound by the reporting interval chosen to balance location precision against battery and data consumption, and the module does not provide tracking continuity in connectivity dead zones. The YOLOv8-based reconciliation mechanism depends on adequate in-van lighting and camera placement, and the prototype demonstration simulates the in-van camera using a laptop webcam rather than dedicated vehicle-mounted hardware. The headcount and ticket-inventory controls raise the cost of unrecorded boarding from a single omission to sustained multi-party collusion, as evidenced in reconciliation data; they detect and deter but cannot fully prevent deliberate collusion among all trip personnel. The two-way messaging module is scoped to in-app text communication among registered platform users and does not include content moderation or message-retention policies; emergency alerts continue to be handled separately through the Twilio API integration described in Section 2.3.5. 

2. # **METHODS**

The project adopts the Scrum Agile framework because SabayGo is a multi-role system with evolving, stakeholder-dependent requirements gathered iteratively from the cooperative, and Scrum's short sprints, product backlog, and sprint reviews allow the four role-based modules (passenger, Conductor, Driver, Operator) to be delivered incrementally with continuous feedback from the terminal manager \[14\]. Empirical software-engineering evidence indicates that Scrum improves software quality and stakeholder responsiveness relative to plan-driven models when requirements change frequently \[14\], which matches the iterative nature of this capstone. Each sprint produces a working increment (e.g., ticketing, then location-based check-in, then the revenue dashboard) that is validated against the interview-derived gaps before the next sprint begins. 

![][image1]

**Figure 1\. Methods Model — Scrum sprint cycle: Product Backlog → Sprint Planning → Sprint Backlog → Sprint (Design–Build–Test) → Sprint Review → Sprint Retrospective**

Figure 1 illustrates the Scrum Agile development process adopted in this study. The methodology consists of iterative sprints that begin with requirements gathering and planning, followed by system design, implementation, testing, review, and deployment. Feedback obtained after every sprint is incorporated into the succeeding development cycle, allowing continuous improvement until the proposed system satisfies all functional and non-functional requirements. 

1. ## **Data Gathering**

The study employed both primary and secondary data collection methods to identify the functional, technical, and regulatory requirements of the proposed SabayGo platform.

Primary data were collected through a key informant interview and an online survey. The principal source was an interview with the manager of the A2Z Transport Cooperative Van Terminal, who served as the study's primary informant on the terminal's existing workflows. The interview documented the current manual processes — handwritten dispatch logbooks, tarpaulin-posted schedules, and informal seat reservations through Facebook Messenger and phone calls — and surfaced the three operational gaps that define this study: revenue leakage arising from walk-in passengers boarded without formal documentation, overloading beyond the 14-seat capacity limit, and the absence of real-time passenger notifications. To complement the interview, a structured questionnaire developed in Google Forms was distributed to thirteen (13) respondents, consisting of employees, students, and daily passengers who represent the intended users of the system. The survey collected information on commuting behavior, terminal-based booking practices, notification preferences, acceptable check-in procedures, and willingness to adopt a mobile booking platform for fixed-route van services. The responses were analyzed to identify the essential features required by potential users.

The researchers also consulted two (2) personnel from the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) Region XI, one Engineer and one Information Technology (IT) Specialist, regarding franchise regulations on fixed routes, vehicle capacity enforcement, and the operational requirements for deploying a booking and fleet management platform within a transport cooperative. These consultations shaped the system's fixed-route scope, capacity-enforcement design, and regulatory compliance features.

Secondary data were gathered through a review of recent scholarly journals, conference proceedings, and credible institutional publications related to intelligent transportation systems, transit e-ticketing, real-time object detection, fleet management, and database concurrency control. These references served as the theoretical foundation for the YOLOv8-based passenger reconciliation pipeline, the segment-based seat inventory model, and the overall architecture of the SabayGo platform \[1\]–\[13\].

## **2.2	Analysis**

## The Analysis phase focused on identifying and documenting the requirements necessary for the successful development of the SabayGo platform. Information gathered from the key informant interview with the A2Z Transport Cooperative terminal manager and literature review was analyzed to determine the functional requirements, technical specifications, regulatory considerations, and operational constraints of the proposed system. The results of this analysis guided the design of the user interface, database structure, seat-booking logic, and compliance monitoring features presented in the succeeding sections. 

*2.2.1	User Requirements*   
The user requirements define the functions that each user role must be able to perform within the SabayGo platform. These requirements were identified through stakeholder consultations and the operational gap analysis of the current manual terminal workflows. The proposed system accommodates four primary user roles: Operator, Conductor, Driver, and Passenger. Each role has designated responsibilities to ensure the secure, efficient, and transparent operation of the terminal-based platform. 

**Table 2\. User Requirements** 

| User | Requirements |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Operator** | Manage cooperative user accounts, configure fleet units and departure schedules, monitor live boarding manifests, trigger and review YOLOv8-based occupancy reconciliation, review the revenue audit trail to reconcile fares and identify unrecorded boardings, enforce the strict 14-seat capacity constraint across the fleet, monitor the live NAHGM vehicle-tracking map across the fleet, and exchange two-way messages with conductors, drivers, and passengers. |
| **Conductor** | (When assigned to a trip) Access the terminal-facing interface to scan passenger QR codes for boarding validation, digitally log walk-in passengers into the live manifest, operate the offline-capable manifest to cache boarding data locally in dead zones for synchronization upon reconnection, transmit live GPS pings for NAHGM tracking throughout the trip, and exchange two-way messages with passengers, the Driver, and the cooperative administrator. |
| **Passenger** | Register an account, browse fixed terminal-to-terminal routes and schedules, reserve and pay for seats, receive digital QR tickets, complete a location-based check-in at the terminal, view live NAHGM vehicle tracking and node-by-node ETA for their booked trip, exchange two-way messages with the assigned Conductor and the cooperative administrator, and receive real-time push notifications for delays and cancellations. |
| **Driver** | Confirm the onboard passenger count through a single-input in-vehicle interface before departing each staffed terminal, issue pre-registered physical QR tickets to cash-paying walk-in passengers at unstaffed stops, transmit live GPS pings for NAHGM tracking throughout the trip, exchange two-way messages with the Conductor and the cooperative administrator, and remit collected cash against the scanned ticket count; all counts and issuances are automatically reconciled against the live manifest. |

*2.2.3	Functional and Non-functional Requirements*  
*2.2.3.1	Functional Requirements*  
The functional requirements define the core capabilities that the proposed SabayGo platform shall provide to ensure secure, transparent, and auditable terminal-based booking and fleet operations. These requirements were identified through the interview with the A2Z Transport Cooperative terminal manager, consultations with the LTFRB Region XI, the user survey, and the review of related literature. Each functional requirement corresponds directly to the specific objectives presented in Section 1.3.2 and serves as the basis for the system modules and testing activities. 

**Table 5\. Functional Requirements**

| Module | Functional Requirement |
| :---- | :---- |
| User Registration and Role Management | The system shall allow passengers, conductors, and operators to register and manage role-based accounts. The system shall restrict each interface and endpoint to its designated user role. |
| Booking and QR Ticketing | The system shall allow passengers to select a boarding and alighting terminal along a fixed route and reserve a seat for the corresponding segments. The system shall issue a tamper-evident digital QR ticket for every confirmed booking. The system shall price every booking and walk-in against the standard pairwise terminal fare matrix. The system shall record fare payments automatically through the PayMongo payment gateway API, without requiring manual entry of payment details.  |
| Location-Based Check-In | The system shall compute the distance between the passenger's live GPS coordinate and their designated boarding node. The system shall confirm check-in only when the computed distance is within the geofence threshold and shall activate each node's geofence only within the boarding window derived from the trip's departure time. |
| NAHGM Live Tracking and ETA | The system shall capture the van's live GPS coordinate at a fixed reporting interval and compute the Haversine distance to each upcoming route node. The system shall mark a node as reached when the computed distance falls within its defined geofence radius, and shall compute and display a node-by-node ETA otherwise. The system shall flag a trip as delayed and trigger a notification if the computed ETA exceeds the scheduled headway by a configurable threshold. |
| Seat Allocation and Concurrency Control | The system shall assign the lowest-indexed seat available on every segment between the passenger's boarding and alighting stops. The system shall enforce the 14-seat capacity on every route segment using MySQL pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), preventing double-booking under simultaneous requests. |
| YOLOv8 Edge-to-Cloud Passenger Reconciliation | The system shall utilize an IoT edge camera to capture a cabin frame and execute a YOLOv8 model to count physical passengers. The system shall compare this visual headcount against the digital manifest and instantly trigger a revenue leakage alert for the operator if the physical count exceeds the manifested count. |
| Walk-In Audit Mechanism | The system shall automatically create booking records from payment-gateway webhooks without manual entry. The system shall track physical QR ticket booklet inventory per holder, enforcing that tickets issued equal tickets scanned plus tickets remaining. The system shall reconcile driver-confirmed headcounts against the manifest at each departure. The system shall cache walk-in and manifest entries locally on the Conductor's device in connectivity dead zones and synchronize them with the server once reconnected.  |
| Revenue Audit and Notifications | The system shall reconcile every occupied segment-seat against a recorded fare and flag discrepancies per trip. The system shall automatically push real-time delay, cancellation, and boarding notifications to passengers. |
| In-App Messaging | The system shall provide structured two-way messaging threads between passengers and conductors, between conductors and drivers, and between any role and the cooperative administrator. The system shall deliver messages in real time using Firebase and shall indicate read status per message. |

*2.2.3.2  Non-Functional Requirements*   
The non-functional requirements describe the quality attributes that the SabayGo platform must satisfy to ensure secure, reliable, and efficient operation. These requirements define the expected performance and operational characteristics of the system rather than its functional behavior.

**Table 6\. Non-Functional Requirements** 

| Requirement | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| Security | The system shall ensure secure user authentication, encrypted data transmission, and identity verification to protect sensitive user and trip information. |
| Performance | The system shall provide efficient booking processing, geofenced check-in validation, seat allocation, and system response times under normal operating conditions. |
| Reliability | The system shall maintain consistent availability and preserve the accuracy of user, vehicle, and trip records throughout system operation, caching data locally during offline states. |
| Usability | The system shall provide an intuitive and responsive mobile interface that enables users to perform tasks with minimal training or assistance. |

### *2.2.4	Feasibility Requirements*  The feasibility analysis evaluates whether the proposed SabayGo platform can be successfully developed and implemented based on technical, economic, operational, and schedule considerations. This assessment determines the practicality of the proposed system and its capability to satisfy the identified user and regulatory requirements. 

*2.2.4.1  Technical Feasibility*   
The proposed SabayGo platform is technically feasible because it utilizes mature and widely supported technologies, including Flutter, FastAPI, Python, MySQL 8.0, the Google Maps Platform, and Firebase. These technologies provide a stable development environment capable of supporting cross-platform mobile applications, secure backend services, geolocation processing, and transactional database management. The YOLOv8 object-detection model, QR-code ticketing, and multi-segment pessimistic locking can all be implemented using existing, well-documented software libraries (Ultralytics, OpenCV, Flask/FastAPI) and native MySQL InnoDB capabilities, minimizing technical risks during development. The NAHGM module's Haversine distance calculation requires no additional specialized library beyond standard trigonometric functions already available in Python, and the two-way messaging module extends Firebase, a service already integrated into the architecture for Authentication and Cloud Messaging, rather than introducing a new vendor dependency. 

## *2.2.4.2  Economic Feasibility* The proposed system is economically feasible because it primarily utilizes open-source technologies, reducing software licensing costs during development. Operational expenses are limited to cloud hosting, domain registration, third-party payment gateway and API subscriptions, and routine maintenance. Because the platform digitizes the cooperative's existing fare collection rather than introducing new charges, its cost is offset by the revenue it protects: every seat is reconciled against a recorded fare, recovering income currently lost to undocumented walk-in boarding. This operational model minimizes financial overhead while supporting a sustainable pilot implementation with the A2Z Transport Cooperative. Because both the NAHGM tracking module and the two-way messaging module build on Firebase's existing free-tier allocation and the Google Maps Platform already budgeted for geolocation services, their introduction adds no new vendor subscription during the pilot phase; usage-based costs for either service would only become relevant if message volume or GPS-ping frequency scales beyond the pilot fleet's size. 

*2.2.4.3  Operational Feasibility*  
Operational feasibility is achieved through the implementation of role-based access, location-based check-in, and a simplified booking workflow that mirrors the terminal's existing boarding sequence. The platform is designed for pilot deployment with the A2Z Transport Cooperative, allowing Conductors to continue managing walk-in passengers — now digitally logged — while operators monitor live manifests and revenue reports. Because intermediate stops may be served by the driver alone, the audit design does not depend on additional terminal staff: payments route directly to the cooperative's account, physical tickets are self-counting through booklet inventory, and passengers themselves verify issuance since only ticketed boardings carry insurance coverage. The offline-capable Conductor manifest ensures operations continue in connectivity dead zones, and the proposed workflow is designed to be intuitive, reducing the learning curve for terminal personnel while supporting accountability and regulatory oversight.

As a matter of cooperative policy, every fleet van is equipped with an in-van camera for headcount-reconciliation purposes prior to route assignment, making it a fixed condition of vehicle deployment rather than a driver-managed add-on. Since the camera is pre-installed and captures only a privacy-compliant blurred snapshot for passenger-count verification, driver adoption is expected to be low-friction, provided cooperative policy makes clear the footage is used solely for reconciliation and not for general surveillance.

NAHGM tracking's operational feasibility depends on the driver or conductor's mobile device maintaining location services and background permissions active for the duration of the trip; because the same device already handles QR-code scanning and manifest logging, no additional hardware is introduced. The GPS reporting interval is tuned to preserve node-level ETA precision while limiting battery and data consumption over a full route rotation. For the two-way messaging module, role-based conversation scoping restricts which roles may initiate a thread with which other roles — for instance, preventing passengers from messaging drivers directly during transit — and because the interaction pattern mirrors the Messenger and SMS channels the terminal already relies on informally, adoption is expected to require minimal additional training.

## *2.2.4.4   Schedule Feasibility* The development of SabayGo is considered schedule-feasible through the adoption of the Scrum Agile Framework, which divides the project into iterative development sprints. Each sprint focuses on the design, implementation, testing, and refinement of specific system modules, allowing continuous stakeholder feedback and progressive improvement throughout the development lifecycle. This iterative approach minimizes project risks and supports the timely completion of the proposed system.

**Figure 2\. SabayGo SDLC schedule chart**

It presents the sprint-based timeline for SabayGo, covering the design, development, and testing phases of the system. 

## 2.3	Design

*2.3.1	Conceptual Framework*   
The system follows an Input–Process–Output (IPO) model. Inputs are passenger booking requests (boarding and alighting terminals), passenger GPS coordinates at check-in, continuous GPS pings from the driver or conductor's device for NAHGM tracking, fleet and schedule data (units, departure times, 14-seat capacity), the route stop sequence, the pairwise terminal fare matrix, payment-gateway confirmations, physical ticket issuances, driver-confirmed headcounts, live in-van camera frames for YOLOv8 passenger detection, and message content submitted by any role for in-app communication. Processes are location-based check-in validation within the designated boarding window, segment-based seat-availability checking and assignment, multi-segment MySQL pessimistic locking for seat reservation, QR-code generation and validation, YOLOv8-based in-van passenger detection and count reconciliation, walk-in audit reconciliation (webhook auto-recording, ticket-inventory balancing, and headcount comparison), Haversine distance computation and geofence-based node status evaluation for NAHGM live tracking, and two-way message routing and delivery. Outputs are digital QR tickets, per-stop live boarding manifests, revenue reconciliation reports, discrepancy alerts, a live vehicle position feed with node-by-node ETA, delivered two-way messages, and real-time delay and cancellation notifications. 

![][image3]

**Figure 3\. SabayGo IPO Conceptual Framework**

INPUT — The input stage consists of all data required for the operation of the proposed SabayGo platform. Operators configure the initial parameters by inputting fleet and schedule data, which includes vehicle units, fixed departure times, the strict 14-seat capacity constraint, and the standard terminal-to-terminal fare matrix. Passengers provide their specific booking requests by selecting their desired routes and schedules, and subsequently supply their live smartphone GPS coordinates during the check-in phase. Additionally, Conductors provide input by logging walk-in passengers directly into the system's terminal-facing interface, drivers confirm onboard passenger counts before each staffed departure, and the cooperative's payment gateway supplies automatic payment confirmations for walk-in transactions, ensuring every boarding enters the formal record. Throughout the trip, the assigned driver or conductor's device supplies a continuous stream of GPS coordinate pings for NAHGM tracking, and any registered user may submit message content through the in-app messaging module, both of which enter the system independently of the booking and reconciliation inputs described above. 

PROCESS — The process stage manages the core transactions and validations of the system. When booking requests or walk-in entries are submitted, the system executes MySQL pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) to manage concurrency; this securely prevents double-booking and enforces the hard 14-seat capacity limit. During passenger boarding, the system verifies the passenger's live GPS location against the registered coordinates of their designated boarding terminal to confirm physical presence, then applies a segment-based seat-availability check to assign the passenger to the next available seat across their required route segments. The walk-in audit reconciliation runs alongside these validations: payment-gateway confirmations create booking records automatically, physical ticket issuances are balanced against booklet inventory, and driver-confirmed headcounts are compared against the expected manifest for each departing segment. Concurrently, the system triggers the YOLOv8-based AI inference layer on operator request to capture and analyze live cabin footage, computing the physical passenger count and comparing it against the digital manifest to flag any variance; it also handles QR-code generation and validation for digital ticketing, and executes an offline caching and synchronization routine to preserve the Conductor's live manifest functionality in connectivity dead zones. Independently of these transactions, the NAHGM module continuously computes the Haversine distance between each van's most recent GPS ping and its next unvisited route node, evaluating whether that distance falls within the node's geofence radius to mark the node as reached or to compute a node-by-node ETA. In parallel, the messaging module routes submitted message content to the appropriate conversation thread and delivers it in real time to the intended recipient roles. 

OUTPUT — The output stage produces the final transactional records, digital assets, and administrative data generated by the platform. For passengers, the system outputs tamper-evident digital QR tickets and triggers automated real-time push notifications regarding boarding status, delays, and trip cancellations. For terminal operations, it generates live boarding manifests that update dynamically as passengers check in or walk-ins are logged. Finally, for cooperative management, the platform outputs comprehensive revenue reconciliation reports, automatic discrepancy alerts, and an auditable per-seat tracking trail, allowing operators to immediately identify unrecorded boardings, reconcile fare collection, and monitor fleet utilization. The platform additionally outputs a live vehicle position feed with node-by-node ETA to the Operator's live map view and to passengers on that trip, and delivers two-way messages across the messaging module's active conversation threads. 

### *2.3.2 Machine Learning and Geolocation-Based Pipelines* 

SabayGo relies on two independent, continuously operating pipelines to close the accountability and visibility gaps that the manual terminal system leaves open: passenger headcount detection using YOLOv8, which validates the physical passenger headcount against the digital manifest to expose revenue leakage, and NAHGM (Node-Aligned Haversine Geofenced Monitoring), which tracks the van's live position against its assigned route nodes to provide real-time visibility and arrival estimation. Both pipelines operate independently of the booking workflow and of each other, and both feed their outputs into the Operator dashboard described in Section 2.3.5. 

*2.3.2.1 Passenger Headcount Detection Using YOLOv8*

This pipeline adapts YOLOv8, a real-time object detection model, into the system's central mechanism for verifying passenger headcounts and catching revenue leakage. Because passenger booking in SabayGo is a straightforward reservation process, the burden of detecting undocumented boardings falls entirely on this pipeline: it independently counts the physical occupants of the van and cross-validates that count against the digital manifest, closing the gap that manual paper logs leave open.

Revenue Auditing and Occupancy Validation. A transport cooperative cannot fully secure its revenue if conductors or drivers bypass the digital system to pocket cash fares. To close this gap, the system relies on an in-van AI inference layer utilizing a YOLOv8 object detection model. This model acts as an automated passenger counting system, verifying capacity constraints and comparing live physical headcounts against the immutable digital baseline.

**How YOLOv8 counts a passenger.** Although YOLOv8 is a pretrained model rather than one built from scratch for this study, how it processes a frame still matters, since it is the mechanism that catches what the manual system cannot: an undocumented walk-in. YOLOv8 scans an entire video frame in a single pass, using a series of convolutional layers to extract visual features, combining that information to detect objects of different sizes, and finally predicting the location and class of each object it finds \[20\]. Unlike earlier YOLO versions, YOLOv8 predicts an object's location directly from its center point instead of comparing against a fixed set of predefined box shapes, which simplifies the model and speeds up the counting step \[20\].

This general detection process is applied here to count human passengers inside a moving van cabin — the same core task a 2024 study applied to public buses, where YOLOv8 was used to automatically count boarding passengers from front- and rear-facing cabin cameras and reported reliable detection accuracy under normal lighting conditions \[21\]. SabayGo adapts this same process to the fixed 14-seat capacity of Philippine UV Express vans: each passenger the model detects becomes one unit toward the visual headcount (C\_visual), which the system compares against the digital manifest (C\_booked) to compute the variance (Δ) described below. Because this detection process runs independently of anything a conductor enters into the system, it cannot be fooled by an omitted logbook entry the way the manual process can — the model does not know what was booked, only what it can see in the frame.

*![][image4]*

**Figure 4\. YOLOv8 Passenger Headcount Detection Pipeline** 

**Reconciliation formula:**

Δ \= C\_visual − C\_booked  
Δ \= 0 → Reconciled  
Δ ≠ 0 → Discrepancy Detected (Audit Required) 

Where C\_visual is the physical passenger count detected by the YOLOv8 model, C\_booked is the manifested ticket count retrieved from the database, and Δ is the variance.

To demonstrate the YOLOv8 reconciliation process, the study uses a sample trip monitored across different segments.

**Table 7\. Sample YOLOv8 Headcount Reconciliation Data** 

| Trip Segment | Digital Manifest (C\_booked) | YOLOv8 Count (C\_visual) | Variance (Δ) | Resolution Status |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Terminal Departure | 12 | 12 | 0 | Reconciled |
| Mid-Route Capture | 12 | 14 | \+2 | Pending |
| Alighting Node | 10 | 10 | 0 | Reconciled |

**Phase 1: Edge Capture and Transmission.** During an active trip, the in-van IoT camera captures live cabin frames. These image frames are transmitted securely from the Client & Edge Layer over HTTP/REST requests to the Python/FastAPI Server Layer.

**Phase 2: AI Inference.** The uploaded image data is routed to the AI Inference Microservice. The YOLOv8 model analyzes the frame to extract the physical headcount (C\_visual). The annotated snapshot, displaying the bounding boxes around detected passengers, is then passed directly to the Infrastructure Layer to serve as visual proof of the cabin's occupancy.

**Phase 3: Variance Calculation and Database Logging.** Once C\_visual is determined, the Application Layer queries the MySQL 8.0 Database Layer to retrieve the current digital manifest count (C\_booked) corresponding to that specific ScheduleID. The system computes the variance (Δ). The audit transaction is then securely logged into the Yolov8\_audit\_logs entity, storing the CapturedAt timestamp, both passenger counts, the calculated variance, and the SnapshotURL pointing to the cloud-stored inference image.

**Phase 4: Conductor Alert and Resolution.** If Δ ≠ 0, the system flags the transaction and restricts the ResolutionStatus to 'Pending'. A discrepancy alert is immediately triggered on the operator's revenue reconciliation dashboard. The operator can then utilize the management interface to review the audit trail, visually verify the unrecorded boardings using the captured snapshot, and mandate that the driver or conductor formally log the walk-in passengers to clear the anomaly and remit the collected cash fare.

#### *2.3.2.2 NAHGM Live Tracking and Geofenced ETA Pipeline*

The NAHGM (Node-Aligned Haversine Geofenced Monitoring) pipeline adapts a continuous geolocation-monitoring workflow into the system's central visibility mechanism for terminal dispatch and passenger transparency. Because the current manual system communicates trip status only through static tarpaulins and informal dispatcher relay, no party outside the van has a reliable way to confirm its live position or arrival estimate once it departs the terminal. This pipeline independently and continuously computes the van's proximity to each upcoming route node, closing the visibility gap that static, manually posted schedules leave open.

Live Visibility and Arrival Estimation. A transport cooperative cannot resolve passenger uncertainty or terminal-side dispatch confusion if the only available trip status is a departure time posted at the terminal. To close this gap, the system relies on a NAHGM module that continuously retrieves the van's live GPS coordinate and calculates its Haversine distance to each node in the assigned route's ordered stop sequence. This module acts as an automated proximity-monitoring system, converting raw coordinate data into a live position feed and a node-by-node estimated time of arrival (ETA).

**How NAHGM tracks a van.** Unlike YOLOv8, NAHGM is not a machine learning model — it is a geometry-based calculation that runs continuously for as long as a trip is active. At its core, NAHGM repeatedly answers one question: how far is the van, right now, from the next stop on its route? To answer this, the system takes two GPS coordinates — the van's current position and the position of the upcoming terminal node — and calculates the straight-line distance between them across the curved surface of the Earth using the Haversine formula, a standard method for computing distance between two latitude-longitude points whose accuracy depends on the reliability of the underlying GPS signal \[13\].

This distance is then compared against a fixed geofence radius set for that node: if the van is close enough, the node is marked as reached and the system begins tracking distance to the next node in the route; if not, the system estimates how long the remaining distance will take based on the van's recent average speed, producing the live ETA passengers see in the app. This repeating cycle — measure distance, check the geofence, update the ETA — is what replaces the terminal's static tarpaulin schedule with something that reflects what is actually happening on the road, using only the GPS signal already available on the driver or conductor's phone.

**![][image5]**

**Figure 5\. NAHGM Live Tracking Pipeline** 

**Haversine distance formula (expanded):**

a \= sin²(Δφ ÷ 2\) \+ cos(φ1) × cos(φ2) × sin²(Δλ ÷ 2\)  
c \= 2 × atan2(√a, √(1 − a))  
d \= R × c

Where φ1 and φ2 are the latitudes of the van and the target route node, expressed in radians; Δφ is the difference between the two latitudes; Δλ is the difference between the two longitudes, in radians; R is Earth's mean radius (≈ 6,371 km); and d is the resulting great-circle distance between the van and the node.

**Geofence and ETA decision logic:**

  d ≤ r\_geofence → Node Reached  
      d \> r\_geofence → En Route (ETA \= d ÷ v\_avg)

Where r\_geofence is the fixed geofence radius defined for that node, v\_avg is the van's smoothed average speed derived from consecutive GPS pings, and ETA is the estimated time of arrival at that node.

To demonstrate the NAHGM tracking process, the study uses a sample trip monitored across different route nodes.

**Table 8\. Sample NAHGM Live Tracking Data**

| Route Node | Distance to Node (d) | Geofence Radius | ETA | Status |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Ecoland Terminal (Origin) | 0 m | 50 m | 00:00 | Reached |
| Km 14 Checkpoint (Mid-Route) | 850 m | 100 m | 00:04 | En Route |
| Cotabato City Terminal (Destination) | 1,400 m | 50 m | 00:07 | En Route |

**Phase 1: GPS Ping Capture and Transmission.** During an active trip, the driver or conductor's mobile device captures its live GPS coordinate at a fixed reporting interval and transmits it securely over HTTP/REST to the FastAPI Server Layer.

**Phase 2: Haversine Distance Computation.** The Application Layer retrieves the assigned route's ordered node sequence for that ScheduleID and computes the Haversine distance between the van's most recent coordinate and its next unvisited node.

**Phase 3: Node Status Evaluation and ETA Logging.** If the computed distance falls within the node's defined geofence radius, the system marks that node as reached and advances tracking to the next node in the sequence; otherwise, it computes an ETA using the van's smoothed average speed and logs the position, distance, and ETA into a live-tracking entity, detailed in Section 2.3.4 (Data Dictionary).

**Phase 4: Operator and Passenger Visibility Update.** The live position feed and node-by-node ETA are pushed to the Operator's live map view and to the Passenger interface, giving both parties continuous visibility into the van's progress without relying on the terminal's static tarpaulin schedule or informal relay. If the computed ETA to a node exceeds the scheduled headway by a configurable threshold, the system flags the trip as Delayed and triggers an automatic push notification through the existing Firebase Cloud Messaging channel (Section 1.3.2.5).

| BirthDate | DATE | NOT NULL | Used by the frontend to dynamically calculate the conductor's current age. |
| PhoneNumber | VARCHAR(15) | UNIQUE, NOT NULL | Direct mobile contact (e.g., \+63 917 123 4567). |
| Gender | ENUM | NOT NULL | Strict values: 'Male', 'Female', 'Other', 'Prefer not to say'. |
| HomeAddress | VARCHAR(255) | NOT NULL | Full residential address of the conductor. |
| ProfilePicUrl | VARCHAR(255) | NULL | CDN link to the uploaded profile picture. |
| AssignedTerminalID | VARCHAR(32) | FK, NOT NULL | Links to the Terminals table for their primary workplace. |
| EmploymentStatus | ENUM | NOT NULL, DEFAULT 'Active' | Strict UI dropdown values: 'Active', 'Suspended', 'Inactive'. |

**Table 21\. Terminals table**

Defines the physical transport hubs used as origin and destination nodes for geofenced proximity matching and fixed-route scheduling.

| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| TerminalID | VARCHAR(32) | PK, NOT NULL | Unique alphanumeric identifier for the terminal. |
| TerminalName | VARCHAR(255) | NOT NULL | e.g., "Ecoland Terminal", "Cotabato City Terminal". |
| City | VARCHAR(100) | NOT NULL | City location for regional grouping. |
| Latitude | DECIMAL(8, 6\) | NOT NULL | Geolocation node for proximity matching. |
| Longitude | DECIMAL(9, 6\) | NOT NULL | Geolocation node for proximity matching. |
| IsActive | BOOLEAN | NOT NULL, DEFAULT TRUE | Marks if the terminal is currently operational. |

### 

### 

### *2.3.5	Architecture Design* SabayGo utilizes a structured, multi-tier client–server architecture engineered for secure concurrent transaction handling and event-driven AI auditing. The Client/Frontend Layer is divided into two distinct interfaces: a Flutter cross-platform mobile application (using the MVVM pattern) for Passengers, Conductors, and Drivers, and a Web Application serving as the Operator command center. The mobile client integrates the Google Maps SDK for node-based route visualization and live NAHGM tracking display, transmits periodic GPS pings from the Driver or Conductor device for NAHGM computation, exchanges two-way messages through the in-app messaging module, and uses Firebase Authentication for secure access. At the edge layer, an in-van IoT camera captures cabin snapshots triggered by door closures or specific GPS nodes to initiate physical audits. 

The Server/Backend Layer is built on Python and FastAPI, utilizing Clean Architecture and Domain-Driven Design (DDD). The backend isolates core business rules from the Infrastructure Layer \[22\], \[23\]; the Domain Layer specifically houses the NAHGM algorithm, which computes the Haversine distance between each van's live GPS coordinate and its next route node to evaluate geofence status and node-by-node ETA. To combat revenue leakage, the system integrates an AI Inference Microservice running the YOLOv8 object detection model. This pipeline processes incoming camera frames to count physical passengers, returning a visual headcount (Cvisual) and a privacy-compliant blurred snapshot to the core backend for discrepancy calculation against the digital manifest (Cbooked). 

To support persistent storage and specialized operations, the backend interacts with a MariaDB Database Layer utilizing the InnoDB storage engine. This ensures transactional integrity via row-level pessimistic locking, structurally managing user profiles, YOLOv8 audit logs, NAHGM tracking logs, conversation and message records, transaction records, and trip histories \[13\]. For offline manifest caching, the Driver client persists the active trip manifest and walk-in entries to a local on-device store in connectivity dead zones; queued mutations are replayed to the FastAPI synchronization endpoint upon reconnection, where server-side pessimistic locking resolves any capacity conflicts. Finally, the infrastructure integrates with external services to extend functionality: the PayMongo API for automated digital fare collection, Firebase for background push notifications (FCM) and real-time two-way message delivery, and the Twilio API to dispatch SMS alerts during SOS emergencies.
